skill.name: fixing-accessibility
skill.description: Audit and fix HTML accessibility issues including ARIA labels, keyboard navigation, focus management, color contrast, and form errors. Use when adding interactive controls, forms, dialogs, or reviewing WCAG compliance.
skill.summary: Find common web accessibility failures and propose minimal, targeted fixes.

content.user_title: Fix Accessibility Issues in Web Interfaces
content.value_statement: Web interfaces often exclude users through missing labels, weak keyboard support, and incorrect focus behavior. This skill audits common accessibility failures and proposes minimal, targeted fixes.
actual_capabilities: Reviews UI files for accessible names, semantic HTML, keyboard access, and visible focus.
Identifies dialog requirements for initial focus, focus trapping, Escape handling, and trigger restoration.
Checks form labels, helper text, required states, invalid states, and error associations.
Evaluates announcements, contrast-dependent states, media alternatives, and reduced-motion support.
Produces quoted violations, concise impact explanations, and targeted code-level fixes.
limitations: Provides rule-based guidance but does not run automated accessibility scanners or browser tests.
Cannot confirm rendered contrast, focus order, or assistive technology behavior without runtime evidence.
Covers common HTML and ARIA concerns, not every WCAG success criterion.
Complex widgets may require established accessible libraries and manual testing.

use_cases.title: Repair a UI Component
use_cases.description: Review a component for missing names, incorrect semantics, keyboard barriers, and focus issues before release.

use_cases.title: Review Form Accessibility
use_cases.description: Check labels, required states, helper text, validation errors, and announcements across a user journey.

use_cases.title: Assess an Interaction Pattern
use_cases.description: Evaluate a dialog, menu, or dropdown and identify requirements for keyboard access and focus management.

prompt_templates.title: Check Accessible Names
prompt_templates.prompt: Review {file} for missing accessible names and incorrect native semantics. Quote each issue and propose a minimal fix.
prompt_templates.scenario: A beginner needs a focused review of buttons, links, and form controls.

prompt_templates.title: Audit a Form
prompt_templates.prompt: Audit the form in {file}. Check labels, helper text, required states, aria-invalid, error associations, and live announcements. Prioritize critical failures.
prompt_templates.scenario: A developer is preparing a form for accessibility testing.

prompt_templates.title: Review Keyboard and Focus
prompt_templates.prompt: Review {files} for keyboard and focus behavior. Check Tab access, visible focus, Escape handling, focus trapping, initial focus, and focus restoration.
prompt_templates.scenario: A team needs to validate a dialog or custom interaction.

prompt_templates.title: Run a Prioritized Audit
prompt_templates.prompt: Perform a prioritized accessibility audit of {scope}. Cover every listed rule category, preserve the architecture, and provide targeted fixes for verified violations.
prompt_templates.scenario: An advanced reviewer needs a broad audit with minimal implementation changes.

output: Violation: The button has no accessible name.
Impact: Screen reader users cannot identify its purpose.
Fix: Add an accessible label and hide the decorative icon.

output_examples.input: Check a dialog that closes without restoring focus.
output: Violation: Focus is lost when the dialog closes.
Impact: Keyboard users may not know where interaction resumed.
Fix: Return focus to the control that opened the dialog.

output_examples.input: Review a form error shown beside an email field.
output: Violation: The error message is not associated with the field.
Impact: Assistive technology may not announce the validation problem.
Fix: Link the error text to the field and expose the invalid state.

best_practices: Test fixes with keyboard navigation, browser accessibility tools, and at least one screen reader.
Prefer native HTML elements before adding ARIA roles or custom keyboard behavior.
Make minimal changes and verify that each fix preserves existing interactions.
anti_patterns: Do not add ARIA when native HTML already provides the required semantics.
Do not remove focus outlines without a clear visible replacement.
Do not refactor unrelated components during a focused accessibility repair.

faq.question: Does this skill guarantee WCAG compliance?
faq.answer: No. It covers common failures, but complete compliance requires broader testing, documentation, and expert review.

faq.question: Can it test a rendered interface?
faq.answer: Not by itself. Provide browser results or runtime evidence when visual contrast, focus order, or assistive technology behavior matters.

faq.question: Does it support React or other frameworks?
faq.answer: Yes. The guidance applies to generated HTML and interaction behavior, while fixes should follow the existing framework patterns.

faq.question: Will it replace custom widgets?
faq.answer: Only when a native element is the appropriate minimal fix. Complex widgets should use established accessible primitives.

faq.question: How are findings prioritized?
faq.answer: Accessible names, keyboard access, focus behavior, and tool boundaries come first. Semantics, forms, announcements, contrast, media, and motion follow.

faq.question: What should I provide for a review?
faq.answer: Provide the relevant UI files, expected interaction behavior, and any known test results. Include related components when focus or announcements cross file boundaries.
